agency: New York City Police Department (NYPD); exams run by NYC Department of Citywide Administrative Services (DCAS)
union: Police Benevolent Association of the City of New York (PBA)
title_code_or_exam: Police Officer, DCAS Exam Nos. 7311-7322 (application periods July 1, 2026 to June 14, 2027)

hiring.summary: Candidates take a free, computer-based civil service exam, offered roughly monthly, and are ranked on an eligible list that usually lasts four years. When their number is reached, the NYPD puts them through medical, psychological, physical and character screening before appointing them to about six months of Police Academy training and a two-year probation.

nodes.title: Apply for the Police Officer exam
nodes.body: The Department of Citywide Administrative Services (DCAS) opens a new Police Officer exam about once a month, applied for online through its Online Application System. The current notice (exams 7311-7322) charges no application fee; a $75 fingerprint fee is due at the investigation stage.
nodes.time: About 2-week application window, monthly from July 2026 to June 2027

nodes.title: Meet the entry requirements
nodes.body: By appointment a candidate needs a high school diploma plus 24 college credits (2.0 average) or two years of honorable full-time military service, U.S. citizenship and a valid New York State driver license. The candidate must be at least 17 to test, at least 20 years and 6 months to be appointed, and must not have turned 35 by the first day of the application period; military time can reduce the counted age by up to seven years. State law sets a floor of 20 and a ceiling of 43 and lets cities set stricter limits.
nodes.time: Residency and license can be met within 30 days of appointment
nodes.law: Civil Service Law § 58; Public Officers Law residency rule cited in the exam notice

nodes.title: Take the computer-based test
nodes.body: The multiple-choice test is taken at a DCAS computer-based testing center. A score of at least 70% is needed to pass.
nodes.time: Testing runs about 2 to 3 weeks after the application window closes

nodes.title: Get ranked on the eligible list
nodes.body: Passing candidates are placed on an eligible list in final score order. Veterans' preference and legacy credits (for a parent or sibling who died in the line of duty) can be added, as can 10 points for New York City residency; all must be claimed before the list is established.
nodes.time: DCAS says a list is usually active for four years; state law allows one to four years

nodes.title: Be certified and selected
nodes.body: DCAS certifies names from the list in rank order to the Police Department, which must choose from among the three highest-standing candidates willing to accept.

nodes.title: Complete candidate assessment
nodes.body: At the NYPD Candidate Assessment Center the candidate goes through character pre-screening and fingerprinting, a medical exam, written and oral psychological exams, a background investigation, a drug and alcohol screening and the Job Standards Test, a six-station physical test that must be finished in 4 minutes 28 seconds.
nodes.time: NYPD says hiring takes 6 months to 1 year on average, and anywhere from 2 months to 4 years

nodes.question: Does the candidate pass every phase?

nodes.title: Removed from consideration
nodes.body: Felony and domestic violence misdemeanor convictions are statutory bars. Before disqualification, state law requires a written statement of reasons and a chance to respond; the NYPD can ask DCAS to remove a candidate who fails the psychological or moral character standards, and DCAS must comply.

nodes.title: Appointed and sent to the Police Academy
nodes.body: The candidate is appointed a probationary police officer and trains at the Police Academy.

nodes.title: Serve probation
nodes.body: Every original appointment is probationary. For police officers, entry-level probation is two years of full-duty status, and the officer is drug tested at the end of it. It can be extended by six months for an investigation, a disciplinary matter or poor performance, and it is also lengthened day for day by time off full duty.
nodes.time: 24 months of full duty, plus up to 6-month extension
nodes.law: Civil Service Law § 63; Personnel Rules 5.2.1 and 5.2.8

nodes.title: Tenured police officer
nodes.body: After completing probation the officer can be disciplined or fired only on written charges after a hearing, with the police commissioner deciding the penalty.

end_to_end.text: Application and testing take about a month and a half. Per the NYPD, the hiring process that follows averages 6 months to 1 year (as short as 2 months, as long as 4 years). Then come about 6 months of academy training within a 24-month probation, so tenure usually comes at least three years after the test.

firing.summary: A probationary officer can be dismissed without a hearing unless the firing is in bad faith. A tenured officer can be fired only on written charges brought within 18 months (no limit for crimes), prosecuted by the NYPD or, for civilian complaints of force, abuse, discourtesy or offensive language, by the CCRB, and tried before an NYPD trial commissioner. The police commissioner alone decides the penalty, which can be reviewed only in state court.

nodes.title: An allegation is investigated
nodes.body: Complaints of excessive force, abuse of authority, discourtesy or offensive language (known as FADO) go to the independent Civilian Complaint Review Board (CCRB). Corruption and other misconduct are investigated by the NYPD, led by the Internal Affairs Bureau. Criminal cases can run in parallel with district attorneys.
nodes.time: No statutory deadline for the investigation itself, but see the 18-month charging limit

nodes.question: Is the officer still on entry-level probation?

nodes.title: Dismissed without a hearing
nodes.body: The Police Department can summarily dismiss a probationary officer without a formal hearing, including for conduct that would not get a tenured officer fired. The Risk Management Bureau makes the recommendation to the police commissioner, and DCAS rules let an agency head end an unsatisfactory probationer's employment by written notice.
nodes.time: Any time during the 2-year probation or its extension
nodes.law: Personnel Rules 5.2.7 and 5.2.8; Matter of Swinton v Safir (1999)

nodes.title: Limited court review
nodes.body: The Court of Appeals has held that a probationary officer can be let go for almost any reason, or none, unless the firing was in bad faith or for an improper reason. The only way to challenge it is a CPLR Article 78 petition filed within four months.

nodes.title: CCRB's Administrative Prosecution Unit prosecutes
nodes.body: The CCRB drafts charges, which the Department Advocate serves on its behalf, and its Administrative Prosecution Unit tries the case. The police commissioner can keep a case away from the CCRB only where there is a related criminal probe or, for an officer with a clean record, where prosecution would not serve the interests of justice. The CCRB can object within five business days and the commissioner can override within five more.
nodes.time: 5 business days to object; 5 to override

nodes.title: Department Advocate's Office prosecutes
nodes.body: The NYPD Department Advocate's Office reviews substantiated allegations, files charges and specifications and prosecutes the case.

nodes.title: Charges served within 18 months
nodes.body: Written charges must be brought within 18 months of the misconduct. That limit does not apply if the conduct would be a crime.

nodes.title: Possible suspension without pay
nodes.body: While charges are pending the commissioner can suspend the officer without pay for up to 30 days. An officer who is not found guilty gets back pay.

nodes.title: Settle or go to a department trial
nodes.body: The officer can settle or take the case to a public trial before the Deputy Commissioner of Trials or an Assistant Deputy Commissioner of Trials. The prosecutor must prove the charges by a preponderance of the evidence, and the trial judge then sends findings and a recommended penalty to the commissioner.
nodes.time: In 2024 the average case was on the trials docket 92 days, and reports followed trials by 29 days on average
nodes.who: Trial commissioner; officer and counsel; prosecutor

nodes.title: Police commissioner decides the penalty
nodes.body: The commissioner has final authority over discipline. Guilty findings can end in termination; forced separation (resignation or retirement, including vested-interest retirement, in lieu of termination); or dismissal probation, where the firing is deferred for a year and any new misconduct in that year can mean summary dismissal. The penalty matrix is advisory, and deviations must be explained in writing and reported each year. Under a 2006 Court of Appeals ruling, discipline cannot be bargained into arbitration.
nodes.law: NYC Charter § 434; Admin Code §§ 14-115, 14-186; PBA v PERB (2006)

nodes.title: Court review under Article 78
nodes.body: A fired officer can challenge the commissioner's final decision in state court under CPLR Article 78 within four months after it becomes final. A felony conviction, or conviction of a crime that violates the oath of office, vacates the job by operation of law, without a separate disciplinary case.

stats.text: The NYPD forcibly separated 56 members of the service in 2024, down from 78 in 2023. The count includes post-trial terminations, felony-conviction dismissals, probationary dismissals, dismissal-probation dismissals and negotiated forced separations, for uniformed and civilian members alike.
From 2022 to 2024, cases the Department Advocate's Office prosecuted closed in 420 days on average; those prosecuted by the CCRB's Administrative Prosecution Unit took 618.

In 2024, 231 new matters were filed with the Deputy Commissioner of Trials and 234 closed. Cases the trials office submitted to the commissioner that year ended in 93 trial dispositions and 141 settlements, with another 15 officers resigning while their cases were active.
In the fourth quarter of 2025 the CCRB's Administrative Prosecution Unit recorded 11 trial verdicts, 98 pleas and 2 cases retained by the police commissioner.

caveats: The NYPD's own pages disagree with the current DCAS exam notice. The FAQ and the older candidate booklet list 60 college credits and a minimum appointment age of 21; the notice for exams 7311-7322 says 24 credits and 20 years 6 months. The flowchart uses the notice, since it governs the exam.

The NYPD hiring and FAQ pages carry 'OLD-' in their URLs. They were live on 2026-09-11, but some figures (the 6-month academy, the 6-month-to-1-year hiring average) may predate the current exam series.
How far military service can lower a candidate's counted age varies by source: up to 7 years (DCAS notice), up to 6 (Civil Service Law § 58) and 4 to 6 (NYPD booklet).

Quotes from the two Court of Appeals cases (sources 22 and 23) and from the two NYPD web pages (11 and 12) came back through a web-fetch tool that extracts text rather than showing the raw page. Check them against the full opinions before publication. The Swinton quote joins two phrases the court was quoting from earlier precedent.

The Administrative Code and Charter text came from the BetaNYC nyc-charter mirror of the American Legal Publishing code, not from amlegal.com directly; the source URLs point to the amlegal index pages.
Nysenate.gov blocked automated fetches, so state statutes were read on the NewYork.Public.Law mirror.
The penalty guidelines effective Sept. 9, 2024 were the latest version found; no 2025 or 2026 revision turned up in searches.
Stats on case durations and separations include civilian members of the service where noted; they are NYPD-reported figures.
unverified: PBA collective bargaining agreement provisions on discipline: the contract was not fetched from the Office of Labor Relations. The flowchart relies on the 2006 Court of Appeals decision for the bar on bargaining over discipline.

Whether an NYPD officer can appeal to the NYC Civil Service Commission under Civil Service Law § 76 instead of going to court. NYPD officers are disciplined under Admin Code § 14-115 through § 75(3-a), and whether § 76's commission route applies to them was not confirmed, so only Article 78 is shown.
The CCRB-NYPD memorandum of understanding on the Administrative Prosecution Unit: the rules (38-A RCNY §§ 1-41 to 1-46) were read, but the MOU itself was not.
Hiring-time statistics from the Mayor's Management Report were not gathered.
The Public Officers Law provision behind the residency requirement (the exam notice cites 'the New York State Public Officers Law') was not fetched; residency is sourced to the exam notice only.
An NYPD Patrol Guide or Administrative Guide section on the disciplinary process was not fetched; process steps rely on the penalty guidelines and statutes.
